feature: Customer profiles, notes, CSV import and export

shopify.text: Native. Create and edit profiles (name, email, phone, address, tax settings, marketing preferences), internal notes and tags, merge duplicates, delete (not with pending orders or subscriptions), bulk edit of names, tags, marketing subscriptions and metafields, CSV import and export, GDPR erasure requests. A merge keeps notes up to 5,000 characters and tags up to 250; profiles with subscription contracts, vaulted cards or store credit cannot be merged. The page gives no CSV size limits or plan differences.

gap: Built: the Customers list (search by name or email) and a customer page (D35) with figures, orders, subscriptions, emails sent, wishlist, discount group (D108), staff-only custom fields (D120), manual bonus adjustments (D130) and tags added and removed one by one (D296, `addCustomerTagAction()`); staff export one person's data and erase them from the customer page (D162: `privacy-export.ts`, `privacy-erasure.ts`, orders restricted and later anonymised, never deleted, audit-logged without personal data); the owner-only customer CSV export is a D165 job (held in `platform.product-customer-and-order-csv`). Still missing: staff adding a customer or editing their name, email, phone or address (only the shopper can, `customers.ts`), notes with author and time, a tag filter on the list, merging two customers, and a customer CSV import.
criteria: Staff add a customer and edit name, email, phone, address and company details; an email already in the store is refused, every change is written to the audit log, and nothing leaks to another store (integration test).
Staff add and remove notes and tags on a customer; the list filters by tag and the page shows notes with author and time.

Staff merge two customers: orders, subscriptions, wishlists and the bonus ledger move to the one kept, order numbers are untouched, and a merge that would lose a company or subscription link is refused with the reason.
Customers export to CSV and import from CSV through the shared import and export pipeline (dry run, per-line errors, resumable), with spreadsheet formulas neutralised by `toCsv()`.
Staff export one customer's data and erase them (orders kept as bookkeeping law requires, without the link to the person), each logged.

shopify.text: Native. Segments are dynamic, rule-based customer lists (a segment query with filters such as predicted spend tier and email subscription status) that update as customers change; they target Shopify Messaging campaigns. The Winter '26 Edition added segmenting by product categories viewed or purchased. Customer tags are separate and editable on the profile.

gap: D296: staff tag people one by one on the customer page (by address, so guests too; `addTag()`/`removeTag()`, also the AI manager's tag tools, D318), and save segments from rules (orders, money spent, first and last order, RFM group, country, language, customer group, company, account, tag, email consent) joined by all or any, with a live count and a member list for staff with customers:read. A segment is the audience of a broadcast (D297, `broadcasts.ts`, held by `broadcasts.int.test.ts`). Still missing: bulk tagging and a tag filter on the Customers list, a test that a segment's RFM count equals the Customers analytics page's, and a segment as the audience of a campaign or discount (codes and campaigns target customer groups and named customers only). Merged on 2026-10-25 (README rule 8): `analytics.dynamic-segments-for-marketing` was the same Shopify feature (rated full); its criteria and evidence are here.
criteria: Customers carry tags that staff add and remove one by one or in bulk, and the customer list filters by tag (store-scoped, integration test).
An owner saves a segment from rules (orders, total spent, last order date, country, discount group, tag, RFM group, marketing consent) joined by all or any; it shows a live count and a member list.
The RFM rule uses the same function as the analytics page, so a segment 'Champions' has exactly the count the Customers analytics shows (test).
A segment can be chosen as the audience of a campaign, a discount or an email send; a customer who stops matching leaves the audience at send time.
An owner builds a segment from a closed list of filters (orders, spend, last order date, country, customer group, RFM group, subscribed) and saves it per store.
A segment's member count and list update from live data and never include another store's customers.
Marketing consent is a filter, and a segment never reveals a customer to anyone who may not see customers.
A segment is selectable as the audience of a broadcast or automation (wave 5).

history.why: Skeptic recheck: no tags, no saved segments and no audience; RFM counts are the analytics rows and discount groups are assigned by hand; same capability is missing in analytics.dynamic-segments-for-marketing.

D296 (wave 5 unit B): saved rule-based segments over customers and subscribers, counted live with a member list, and customer tags; read segments.ts and ran segments.test.ts, segments.int.test.ts (PGlite and integration, passed).

feature: Email marketing: broadcasts and lifecycle automations

shopify.text: Native (Shopify Email, now in the Shopify Messaging app). The first 10,000 emails each month are free, then $1 per 1,000. Templates, segments, and automations for welcome, abandoned cart, browse abandonment, follow-up, win-back and drip sequences. The Winter '26 Edition adds best-seller blocks in emails.

gap: D295 subscriber list (consent words, time, source, confirmation, language; one-click unsubscribe; export and erasure), D297 broadcasts (written per language from blocks, a test to staff, sent now or scheduled to everyone subscribed or a segment's subscribed people, once each, with List-Unsubscribe headers; hard bounces and complaints unsubscribe; a report of sent, delivered, bounced, complained, unsubscribed and link clicks; AI suggestions pass `findClaims()`), D298 lifecycle automations (welcome, after a delivered purchase, win-back: per store, words per language from hand-written starters, once per person and trigger, subscribed addresses only), and D318's AI manager tools, which save broadcasts as drafts and start or schedule them only behind the `send` gate. Still missing: email templates to start a broadcast from (criterion 2; a broadcast starts blank or from an AI suggestion), product blocks in emails, drip sequences of several emails, browse abandonment, and click counts for automation emails.
criteria: A subscriber list with consent (source, consent text, time, double opt-in time, language) is kept apart from order customers; one-click unsubscribe with List-Unsubscribe headers; export and erase.

An owner writes an email in the store's languages from a template, sends a test to staff, and sends now or later to a segment or all subscribers; only subscribed addresses receive it, once each (idempotency key).
Bounced or complaining addresses are suppressed from later sends (uses the email event log), and each send reports sent, delivered, bounced and unsubscribed.
Lifecycle automations (welcome, post-purchase, win-back) are switched on per store and fire once per person per trigger; cart reminders stay as they are.
No AI-written text reaches a subscriber without passing `findClaims()` and a person's approval (gated send).

history.why: First report's skeptic recheck: abandoned-cart reminders (D33) are real automation and the AI manager can email one customer, so not missing; still no subscriber list, composer or send to a segment. Entry written in wave 0 from the first report, which did not log it.

shopify.text: Native. One automated email a chosen time after the checkout was abandoned, with a link back to the cart; not sent after a purchase, with a payment error, for a phone-only checkout, an unshippable address, free or unavailable products, or a high-risk Shopify Payments attempt. The article describes no discount code and no SMS (SMS abandoned-checkout automations are in Shopify Messaging).

gap: Caveat, not a gap: email only, like the article. Whether a reminder is marketing needs each store's own consent decision (D33 gives the notice and the opt-out).
criteria: A store starts with three reminders (after an hour, a day and three days), each editable in timing, text per language and an optional discount code, and can switch them on or off.
A shopper's email is kept at checkout only after a valid address is typed, with a notice and a way to say no; signed-in customers are not captured.
At most one reminder per cart per run, claimed before it is sent, so none goes twice; reminders stop when the cart is paid, when the same email buys, on opt-out and after 30 days.
The reminder's button puts the same cart back in the shopper's browser; the email and cart are erased on opt-out and 60 days after capture.

shopify.text: Native (Shopify Messaging), pay per send, but limited by country. Recipient countries: Austria (paused from 1 October 2026), Canada, Denmark, Finland, Italy, Luxembourg, Poland, Portugal, Spain (paused from 15 September 2026), Sweden, United Kingdom, United States. Norway is not on the list. Campaigns plus abandoned cart, abandoned checkout and browse abandonment automations.

gap: No SMS channel: no provider, no phone-number consent, no sender id (no SMS code in `src/`). Plan section 5, decision 5 is open: integrate one EU-hosted provider after email broadcasts, which now exist (D297), so the precondition is met. Shopify's own SMS marketing does not reach Norway.
criteria: A decision is recorded (docs/parity-plan.md section 5, decision 5) to integrate one EU-hosted SMS provider or to skip it.
If built: a phone number is collected with explicit SMS consent text, time and source; STOP unsubscribes at once; nothing is sent to a number without consent (test).
Sends respect quiet hours in the recipient's time zone and the country's sender rules, go through the same segments as email, and show their cost, never above an owner-set cap.

feature: Signup forms and popups building a list

shopify.text: Native (Shopify Forms, a free app installed by the merchant). Several forms build the subscriber list, can approve wholesale retailers and learn about visitors; a new or existing discount can be added as an incentive to sign up for email, SMS or WhatsApp; subscribers can be tagged to build segments; analytics and automation triggers. The page does not describe popups, consent or double opt-in.

gap: Caveat: no report of a popup's own views and sign-ups (an A/B test's form goal, D148 phase 11, counts sends), and no welcome code when the owner switched the form's email confirmation off.
criteria: A confirmed newsletter sign-up creates or updates a subscriber (store, email, source form, consent text and time, language, double opt-in time), not only an email to the owner.
A sign-up form or popup can give an incentive: after confirmation a single-use discount code is emailed once per address.
A form can tag its subscribers and the tags are selectable in segments.
A popup built as a modal row opens by its trigger, respects the visitor's remembered choice only after consent, and never shows over a working page.

history.why: Every criterion holds: a confirmed newsletter sign-up keeps a subscriber with consent words, time, source form, language and confirmation (D295, `forms.ts` → `joinList()`, `marketing-subscribers.int.test.ts`); a form's incentive emails one single-use code per store, discount and address after confirmation and its tags are a segment condition (D304 J3, `issueSignupCode()`, `tagFromForm()`, `signup-codes.int.test.ts`, run 2026-10-25, passing); a popup is a D121 modal row whose triggers, after-consent memory and refusal on working pages are held by `page-modal.test.ts` and `e2e/modals.spec.ts`.

shopify.text: Native. Discount types: amount off products or the order (percentage or fixed), Buy X get Y, free shipping; customers enter codes at checkout (or in Shopify POS); discounts can be scheduled. Combinations are chosen per discount: up to 5 product or order codes and 1 shipping code per order. The overview pages read give no limit on codes, customer eligibility or bulk generation.

gap: Caveat: Buy X get Y is a campaign kind (D299 E4), not a code; a code cannot be limited to a segment (groups and named customers only).
criteria: A code applies to chosen products, categories or tags, and can require a minimum quantity as well as a minimum amount.
A code can be limited to customer groups or chosen customers; one outside the limit is refused with the reason.
An owner generates up to a stated number of unique single-use codes from a pattern and exports them as CSV; each code has its own use count under a row lock.

More than one code per order is allowed within the owner's combination rules, and `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit, in a NOK and a euro scenario (`checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`).

history.why: All four criteria hold (D299 E1, E2): codes reach products, categories and tags with a minimum number of items, are limited to customer groups or named customers, hand out single-use codes exported as CSV and counted under a row lock, and up to five codes combine by `combines_with` with the better one kept otherwise. Held by `discounts.int.test.ts` (run 2026-10-25, passing) and `checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`'s code scenarios including 'goods with two codes that combine, shown in euro' and a single-use code in euro (run with -t code, 11 passing).

shopify.text: Native. Automatic discounts apply without a code (amount off, Buy X get Y, free shipping); up to 25 active automatic discounts per store; each discount sets which classes (product, order, shipping) it combines with, and when they cannot combine the best for the customer is chosen.

criteria: An owner makes an automatic discount of a fixed amount per market off chosen products or the order, and an automatic free-shipping discount above a basket value per market.
An automatic discount can be tiered by spend (spend X get a % off), applied without a code.
`cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit for each new kind, in a NOK and a euro scenario (`checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`).
A product page and card announce the offer from the cached `campaignNotices()` read without a per-request query.

history.why: D299 E3: campaigns of an amount off per market (with an optional threshold), free shipping (with an optional threshold) and tiers by items or spend, held together by `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` in NOK and euro scenarios, announced from the cached notices.

shopify.text: Native, as a code or automatic. The customer buys a minimum quantity or a minimum amount of chosen products or collections and gets a quantity free, a percentage off or an amount off each; a maximum number of uses per order can be set. The free or discounted item is never added to the cart automatically.

criteria: An owner defines a buy set (a quantity or an amount of chosen products, categories or tags) and a get set (a quantity of chosen products) that is free, a percentage off or an amount off, with a maximum number of uses per order.
Buy and get sets may be different products; which units are discounted is stated and tested (cheapest first); each discounted unit's share is on its own order line so VAT and refunds agree.

`cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit, in a NOK and a euro scenario (`checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`), and the offer is left off subscriptions, bookings and appointments as other campaigns are.

history.why: D299 E4: a buy X get Y campaign (a buy set by items or an amount per market, a get set of its own or the same, free, a percentage or an amount off per unit, cheapest first, never a unit counted as bought, uses per order), on its own order lines, held together by `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` in NOK and euro scenarios, and only on goods bought once.

shopify.text: App. Shopify's discount types are amount off, Buy X get Y and free shipping; the page says tiered, volume or spend-more-save-more discounts are not native and need an app from the App Store, Checkout Blocks (Plus only) or a custom app. (The first report's tier was from memory and is confirmed.)

gap: D299 E3: a tiered campaign (two to five steps, by items or by spend per market, the highest step reached applies, never the sum) with its ladder on the product page and how far the next step is in the cart (`nextSteps()`), held in NOK and euro scenarios of `checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`. Still missing: a step that gives an amount off (`tierPercent()`: percentages only), which criterion 1 asks for.
criteria: An owner defines tiers on one discount from quantity or spend thresholds, each with a percentage or amount; the highest tier reached applies, never the sum of tiers.
The product page shows the ladder for that product and the cart says how far the next tier is.
`cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit, in a NOK and a euro scenario, with each line's VAT worked out on what is paid.

history.why: First report's skeptic recheck: overlapping multi-buy campaigns and a stacking percentage approximate a ladder, so not missing; no true spend-more-save-more discount. Entry written in wave 0 from the first report, which did not log it.

shopify.text: Native. Three classes (product, order, shipping); most pairs can combine and two shipping discounts cannot; a customer may use up to 5 product or order codes and 1 shipping code per order; discounts apply product first, then order, then shipping; the merchant sets per discount which classes it combines with, and when they cannot combine the best for the customer wins with the message 'Discount couldn't be used with your existing discounts'. Only Plus can combine several product discounts on one line. Customer targeting by segment is not on the page read.

gap: D299 E2: up to five codes on an order, each saying which kinds of code it combines with (products, order, free shipping, `combines_with`); where two cannot combine the shopper gets the one taking more off and the cart says why (`stackCodes()`); codes are limited to customer groups or named customers (E1). Campaigns may stack with each other (D115 `stacks`) and be limited per group and customer (D115, D116). Still missing: an owner's choice of whether a code combines with campaigns (campaigns always come first, then the group discount, the referral welcome discount, codes and bonus credits, fixed in code), and limiting a code or campaign to a segment.
criteria: An owner chooses per discount which kinds it may combine with (campaign, code, shipping); the defaults equal today's fixed order so nothing changes unasked.
When discounts cannot combine, the one best for the shopper is applied and the cart says why another was not.
A code can be limited to customer groups, chosen customers or a segment, and a shopper outside it is told so.
`cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit for every allowed combination, in a NOK and a euro scenario.

shopify.text: App. Shopify has no built-in 30-day lowest-price display; the listing at this address (Complimus) saves every price daily and shows the lowest price of the last 30 days on discounted products, with Markets and multi-currency support; free for up to 100 products, then from $14.99 a month.

gap: Caveat: the reference shows only where the current price is below the lowest price in the previous 30 days of that market (`prior_30d_minor`); campaign and code discounts are not advertised against a was-price, so they raise no reference-price question.
criteria: A price changes only through `commerce.set_price`, which keeps the history per variant and market.
`commerce.current_prices.prior_30d_minor` is the lowest price that applied in the 30 days before the current price began; a first price has none.
`<Price>` shows the reference only when the current price is lower than it, with the label, in the market's currency and VAT display.

shopify.text: Native. 'Sell gift cards' is listed on every plan (Basic, Grow, Advanced, Plus).

gap: D300: gift cards are sold in fixed amounts (a product of kind gift_card, its variants the amounts), delivered by email to the buyer or a recipient on a chosen day with their message, spent at checkout as payments (never a discount; NOK and euro scenarios agree to the minor unit; a card never pays for a gift card, a subscription, a change or an exchange), refunded back to the card, issued by hand, changed, deactivated and expired by the ledger's functions (balance only from `commerce.gift_card_balance()`), and reported per currency on Finance with its CSV. Still missing: a custom amount the shopper chooses, sending a card's code again after delivery (codes are kept only as hashes); the voucher VAT treatment and the expiry rules wait for an accountant's and a lawyer's review.
criteria: A store sells gift cards in fixed amounts (and an optional custom amount within limits) as a product kind; once paid, a unique code goes by email to the recipient on the chosen day with the sender's message.

A code pays part or all of an order at checkout, the rest of the balance stays, and `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree to the minor unit, in a NOK and a euro scenario; a gift card is never bought with a gift card.
The balance is only ever read from an append-only ledger function like the bonus program's; a refund goes back to the card balance or the original method, never both.
A liability report shows the outstanding balance per currency and equals the ledger's sum (test); expiry is never sooner than the law allows and the VAT treatment is written in the spec.

history.why: Wave 5 unit F (D300): gift cards sold, spent, issued by hand and reported; a custom amount is not built.

shopify.text: App. Shopify has no native loyalty program (store credit is the built-in nearest thing; the Winter '26 Edition announcement does not mention loyalty, so the first report's source did not support the tier). Smile, a typical app, offers points on purchases, VIP tiers, referrals and points for actions such as account creation and birthdays, redeemed as discounts, free shipping, free products or gift cards; free up to 200 orders a month.

gap: The bonus program (D130) earns credits on paid goods (5 % by default) for signed-in customers, holds them pending then usable, expires them, redeems them as a last price reduction and keeps an append-only ledger with refund reversals and manual adjustment. Missing next to a loyalty app: VIP tiers or tier multipliers (listed as not built in `docs/bonus.md`), points for actions (account creation, birthday, review, sign-up) and reward kinds beyond a price reduction (free shipping, free product).
criteria: An owner defines tiers by spend over a window, each with a higher earn rate; a customer sees their tier and the way to the next in My account.
Points are given for actions (account creation, birthday, newsletter confirmation, review when reviews exist), each once per customer through an idempotent ledger key.
A reward can be free shipping or a free product as well as a price reduction, and `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree on it (`checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`).
The ledger stays append-only and balances come only from `commerce.bonus_balance()`.

history.why: Skeptic recheck against the app side: Smile's listing offers VIP tiers and points for actions, and docs/bonus.md lists tier multipliers as not built; D130 covers earn, redeem, expiry and ledger only. The first report's own gap text already said 'no tiers or action points'.

shopify.text: App. Shopify has no native customer-to-customer referral feature (its own Partner and affiliate programmes reward referring merchants). Apps such as ReferTech add refer-a-friend campaigns on the thank-you page and a referral page, a customer dashboard with links and rewards, and fraud checks against self-referral; free for 1 campaign and 50 referrals a year. (The first report's tier was from memory and is confirmed.)

gap: Caveat: rewards are bonus credits, not cash; the friend's welcome discount applies to the first paid order of a signed-in customer; the program works only while the bonus program is on.
criteria: A signed-in customer gets a code and a link; a friend arriving by it gets the welcome discount on a first paid order only, and self-referral or a customer who has ordered before is refused (SQL guards, integration test).
The referrer's reward is a bonus credit lot, pending then usable, reversed on refund or cancellation and cut by the monthly cap.
`cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` agree on the welcome discount to the minor unit, euro scenario included.
A referrer never sees who a friend is, and a staff block stops new earnings without taking back old ones.

shopify.text: Native (Shopify Collabs, a Shopify-built app, free to install). Creator application pages, personalised gifts and discount codes, unique referral links and codes, conversion and commission tracking with tiered, custom and per-product commissions, and automatic payouts through Shopify Billing with a 2.9 % processing fee. The listing is a US company and English; it names no country restrictions, so EU availability is not confirmed.

gap: D131's store program is customers referring friends for a welcome discount and bonus credits, with no approval. Missing: a creator or affiliate application and approval, per-affiliate commission rates paid in money, a commission ledger with payouts, and a dashboard of clicks and sales for the creator.
criteria: A creator applies on a store page (name, email, channel link, consent) and the owner approves or declines; an approved creator gets a code and a link.

A commission (a percentage of paid goods without VAT, optionally per product or category) accrues on paid orders, is reversed on refund and cancellation, and never accrues on copied or host orders (integration test, euro scenario).
The commission ledger is append-only, per currency and never converted; the owner records payouts (Kaizen moves no money) and exports them as CSV.
The creator's dashboard shows clicks, orders and earnings and never a buyer's identity.

shopify.text: Native for Facebook and Instagram (Shopify's channel: catalogue sync for Facebook Shop and Instagram Shopping, Meta Pixel and Conversions API with a chosen data-sharing level, ads). TikTok and Pinterest are free apps built by TikTok Inc. and Pinterest (catalogue sync, TikTok Pixel or Pinterest tag, ads, TikTok Shop orders); their listings name no EU restriction.

gap: Meta, TikTok and Pinterest catalogue CSVs from the same normalised list as the Google feed (D302), at the store's secret address per market, cached 15 minutes and budgeted, with products not for sale left out and named on the admin's page; the pixels and server-side conversions are D303. The channel accounts are the owner's: each fetches the address on its own schedule (a catalogue API sync or TikTok Shop orders would be bucket B).
criteria: One normalised product list produces a Meta catalogue feed, a TikTok catalogue feed and a Pinterest catalogue feed with price with VAT in the market's currency, availability and images; unit-tested against each format.
Products not for sale (draft, unavailable, no price, restricted) are left out with a report of why.
Each feed is a tokenised address per store, market and language, rate-limited and cached, and shows price and stock changes within its stated refresh time.
Live only once the store has connected the channel account and the platform has approved it (bucket B).

history.why: Wave 5 unit H (D302): the three catalogue feeds with the left-out report, beside D303's pixels and conversions.

shopify.text: Native. The Facebook & Instagram channel creates and adds the Meta Pixel, lets the merchant choose the customer data-sharing level and sends events through the Conversions API; the Google & YouTube app adds a conversion-tracking pixel; the TikTok app a TikTok Pixel and the Pinterest app a Pinterest tag.

gap: Caveat: GA4, GTM, Meta, Google Ads, TikTok and Pinterest tags load only after consent (D58, D303 I1) and get view-item, view-item-list, search and add-to-cart in the browser; begin-checkout and purchase go server-side only (D303 I2: Conversions API, Measurement Protocol, Events API, once per order and platform, order id as event id, consented carts only), because pay routes load no third-party script (D158). Not built: Google Ads conversions by API (bucket B) and refund events.
criteria: With consent, the storefront sends view-item, add-to-cart, begin-checkout and purchase events to GA4, GTM's data layer and Meta Pixel with product ids, quantity and value in the order's currency, once per order; before consent nothing is sent (e2e).

A purchase also goes server-side (Meta Conversions API, GA4 Measurement Protocol) with the same event id so it is not counted twice, only for orders whose visitor consented, with hashed email only, never for copied or host orders; the owner's tokens are encrypted.
TikTok and Pinterest tags can be switched on in the tracking settings and are listed in `KNOWN_COOKIES` and loaded only after consent.

history.why: D303 I1 and I2: tags after consent, browser shop events, and server-side checkout and purchase events with consent; the browser purchase is replaced by the server event by design.

shopify.text: Native. Campaigns and activities are created, and their results reviewed, from the Growth page; Shop Campaigns, SEO tools, Collabs and Audiences are listed as ways to market. The page read does not describe UTM setup, attribution windows or spend tracking.

gap: D303 I3: a campaign table per UTM source and campaign (sessions, paid orders, revenue without VAT in the main currency, new customers, spend entered under the campaign's name, CAC, ROAS; CSV `marketing.campaigns`), by the last visit or the first visit in 30 days for visitors who accepted statistics (`kaizen_touch_{store}`, in `KNOWN_COOKIES`; the page says how many orders know their first visit), a campaign-link builder for the store's own addresses, and spend imported from a CSV file. Spend synced from an ad platform needs each platform's credential (bucket B) and is not built.
criteria: A campaign link builder makes UTM-tagged addresses, and visits with `utm_campaign` are reported per named campaign with sessions, orders, revenue and spend.

For visitors who accepted marketing or statistics cookies, attribution covers a stated lookback window through a cookie listed in `KNOWN_COOKIES`; without consent it stays same-day and the report says which it used.
Revenue per campaign is without VAT, in the store's main currency, from paid orders only, never copied or host orders (integration test, euro scenario).
Ad spend can be imported from a CSV; syncing it from an ad platform is bucket B.

history.why: D303 I3: campaign table, last or first visit in 30 days with statistics consent, link builder and spend import, held by analytics-traffic-data.int.test.ts (euro order, copied and host orders out) and analytics-visits.int.test.ts.

shopify.text: App. Shopify's own Product Reviews app was discontinued on 6 May 2024 (existing reviews were removed unless exported as CSV); Shopify points merchants to apps such as Judge.me, AirReviews, Ali Reviews, Kooee Reviews, Vitals and Stamped. (The first report's tier is confirmed.)

gap: Buyers review what they bought and received from My account or the link of the request email the store sends once per order some days after receipt (only to subscribed buyers, with the unsubscribe link), so every written review is a verified purchase; reviews wait in Products → Reviews unless the owner publishes at once, are published, hidden with a reason or answered by staff, who can never change a word or a star, and the product page shows the stars, the average, the newest reviews and how reviews are checked, with aggregateRating in the JSON-LD from published reviews only. Reviews written elsewhere are imported from CSV (marked imported, never verified, a file imported twice adds nothing) and all are exported as CSV. Not yet: pictures in reviews (G4) and stars on product cards.
criteria: A shopper reviews a product with a rating and text; a review is marked verified only when the same account or order email has a paid, delivered order for it (integration test).
New reviews wait in a moderation queue; the owner approves, hides or answers them; nothing is published unmoderated unless the owner chose so.
`aggregateRating` in JSON-LD and any star display count only published reviews of the product, never AI text (unit test).
A review-request email goes out once after delivery, with the store's consent rules and an unsubscribe link; reviews can be imported from CSV.

history.why: Wave 5 unit G steps 1 and 2 (D301): verified-purchase reviews written from My account, checked and answered in the admin, shown with the rating and in the JSON-LD; the request email, imports and pictures follow.

Wave 5 unit G3 (D301): the request email after receipt, to subscribed buyers with the unsubscribe link, and CSV import and export: every criterion met. Pictures (G4) and stars on cards remain in the gap.

shopify.text: App. A community answer says Shopify has not announced a native wishlist; merchants use apps such as Wishlist Guru, Advanced Wishlist and Wishlist Monk (guest wishlists, back-in-stock notifications). (The first report's tier is confirmed.)

gap: Caveat: lists are private, with no way to share one, and nothing is emailed from them (no price-drop mail; back in stock is its own request, D298); at most 20 lists and 200 items per list.
criteria: A heart on every product card and product page saves the product in the shopper's first list (made on the first save) and, tapped again, takes it out of every list.
A shopper keeps several lists, renames and deletes them, and moves all or some of a list into the cart.
A shopper need not sign in: a guest's lists belong to the browser (a hashed token) and join the account at sign-in, merging a list with the same name; lists are visible to no one else.
Staff see every list, what is in it and what went from a list to the cart and was bought (D36).

shopify.text: App. Shopify does not email shoppers when a product is back in stock; apps do (for example Amp Back in Stock, which auto-notifies by email, SMS and push; free for 10 notifications a month, from $19 a month). The first report's source (a changelog about SMS automations) does not mention back-in-stock and has been replaced.

gap: D298: a sold-out physical variant that does not keep selling shows *Email me when it is back* while the store has back in stock on; a typed address confirms from its link first (a verified signed-in customer's waits at once), one open request per store, variant and address, limited per visitor key and address. Each run, waiting requests whose variant is in stock again by any path (`variant_availability`) and still offered get one email each, claimed before it goes; requests are store-scoped, exported, erased and pruned (unconfirmed after 7 days, waiting after 180, sent after 30). Staff see how many wait and the products most asked for, and the AI manager's `list_email_automations` repeats the waiting count (D318, `marketing-tools.ts`). Still missing: the live price in the email and a link in it to cancel a waiting request.
criteria: A sold-out variant shows a notify-me form for an email address with a consent text and double opt-in; one waiting request per email and variant per store.

When a variant's stock rises from 0 above 0 by any path (restock, return, cancelled order), each waiting address gets one email, keyed so none goes twice, showing the live price and stock read at send time.
One-click unsubscribe; a request is erased after it is sent or after 12 months; requests are store-scoped (integration test).
Staff see how many are waiting per product, and an AI-manager or analytics reading of demand uses the same count.

history.why: D298 built the notify-me form with double opt-in, one email per waiting address when stock returns by any path, store scope, export, erasure and pruning, and the staff's waiting counts; the email does not show the live price, a waiting request has no cancel link, and the AI manager does not read the count.

shopify.text: Native. Passwordless sign-in by emailed code, Shop Pay, and Google and Facebook sign-in (external identity provider on Plus only); order history and status, self-serve returns, profile editing with shipping addresses, sessions up to 365 days, auto-filled checkout.

gap: Built (D28, D153, D162, D304): sign-in by emailed code or password; orders, subscriptions, company, bonus and referral pages, wishlist, account deletion; the order page shows withdrawals and returns and links to the withdrawal function; several saved addresses (up to 20, defaults for delivery and billing) offered where checkout asks the address itself (J1, `customer-addresses.ts`); the shopper's own data export after a fresh sign-in (D162, My account → Privacy); *Your orders* searches the customer's own orders by number, product or SKU and tracking number, filters by state and pages (J2, `findCustomerOrders()`). Still missing: social sign-in (criterion 4), which needs an OAuth client per provider (bucket B).
criteria: A customer keeps several saved addresses (add, edit, delete, default), checkout offers them, and they are per customer and store.
A customer downloads their own data (profile, addresses, orders, subscriptions, bonus ledger, wishlists, consents) as a machine-readable file after proving it is them again.
Order history is searchable by order number, product and date and shows only the customer's own orders.
A customer can sign in with Google by a verified email matched to the account, never linking an unverified address (tested against a stubbed provider; live once the OAuth client exists).
A signed-in customer starts a withdrawal or return from the order page (holds today, D153).

shopify.text: Native. Several blogs per store (the help centre has 'Manage blogs'), a built-in blogging engine, and customer comments that can be disabled, held for moderation or auto-published, with automatic spam flagging (replying to comments needs an app).

gap: Verified: one blog per store (`/blog`, articles are pages of type `article`, D57) with author name, categories, tags, search texts, JSON-LD `Article`, translations, versions and draft or publish. Missing: more than one blog, customer comments with moderation, an RSS or Atom feed and scheduled publishing (none in the code).
criteria: A store can have several blogs, each with its own address, listing, categories and tags.

Readers can comment on an article when the owner allows it (off, moderated or automatic); comments set no cookie, are rate-limited by hashed keys, pass a spam check and appear only when approved in the default setting.
Each blog has an RSS or Atom feed that lists only published articles, linked from the page head.
An article can be scheduled to publish at a set time in the store's time zone and is not visible, in sitemaps or in the feed before it.

history.why: Skeptic recheck against Shopify's blog help page: comments with moderation and several blogs are native, and the code has neither (nor an RSS feed or scheduled publishing); docs/parity-plan.md wave 7 lists them as blog depth still to build. The first report's gap text already said 'no comments'.

shopify.text: Native. sitemap.xml and robots.txt are generated automatically, canonical tags are added automatically, themes generate title tags with the store name and include product structured data; merchants edit title tags, meta descriptions and URLs for products, collections, blog posts and pages, and image alt text in the media library; page titles up to 70 characters (60 recommended) and descriptions of about 160.

gap: Caveat: a changed address leaves a permanent redirect since D168 (`storefront.url-redirect-manager`). Evidence debt: e2e holds the description, canonical, hreflang and og:image output and `term-metadata.int.test.ts` the X tags of a category page, but nothing asserts the empty-SEO-field fallback to the product's own title and description (`productText()`) or the store's share tags (`storeShareTags()`).
criteria: Every public page has a title, meta description, canonical and hreflang links for the store's markets, and Open Graph and X tags; a product with empty SEO fields falls back to its own title and description (unit tests).

The sitemap, robots.txt and llms.txt are generated per store, list only an open store's published pages and active products, and follow the owner's crawler rules, which are checked line by line when saved (integration test).

Products, product groups, the store, market home pages and articles carry schema.org JSON-LD (Product or ProductGroup with offers and return policy, WebSite, Article) from the page's own data (unit tests).
A hidden or template store is left out of sitemaps and llms.txt; withdrawal and return-status pages are for no search engine.
